questions.q: What are the three concrete checks that make up scoping an incident?
options: Other accounts accessed, other hosts connected to, and whether data actually left the environment
The original alert's severity, its alert ID, and its queue position
The attacker's name, their physical address, and their motive
The cost of the incident, the CEO's reaction, and the press release wording
questions.explain: Scoping systematically checks lateral reach into other accounts and hosts, plus whether any data was actually exfiltrated.

questions.q: In the example, how was the second SSO sign-in at 9:28am discovered?
options: It appeared automatically in the original timeline from Lesson 10
It was found by resetting the account's password
By deliberately checking the compromised account's full sign-in history across the whole incident window
A user reported it to the help desk
questions.explain: The original timeline, built from the first set of known entities, never surfaced it - only a deliberate scoping check did.

questions.q: What is the common real IR failure pattern this lesson describes?
options: Never resetting a compromised account's password
Spending too much time scoping before doing any containment at all
Scoping every incident even when it is clearly a false positive
Fixing the problem that was found and closing the incident without checking for a second foothold
questions.explain: Resetting a password and rebuilding one server fixes what was found, but a second foothold left unchecked can let the incident reopen later.

questions.q: Why might an incident that reopens due to a missed foothold look like a brand-new case instead of the same attacker returning?
options: Because incident tickets are deleted automatically after being closed
Because the unchecked second system was never tied back to the original incident's scope
Because scoping checks are only valid for 24 hours
Because attackers are required to use a different account every time
questions.explain: Without the scoping check connecting it back, the second foothold's activity has no obvious link to the original, already-closed incident.

questions.q: Why does accurate scoping matter for the severity classification covered in the next lesson?
options: Because scoping and severity classification are unrelated steps
Because severity is assigned before any investigation begins and never changes
Because severity depends on the incident's real scope, which scoping is what actually confirms
Because only the original alert, not the full scope, is used to set severity
questions.explain: Severity decisions depend on knowing the incident's true scope, which is exactly what a completed scoping check establishes.
